nodes.label: Vectors
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A vector is a mathematical object with both magnitude and direction. In Rⁿ, a vector is an ordered list of n numbers called components. Vectors can represent positions, displacements, forces, velocities. Two vectors are equal only if all components are equal. The zero vector has magnitude 0. Geometrically, vectors are arrows in space.

nodes.label: Vector Operations
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Vectors support addition (component-wise), subtraction, and scalar multiplication. Vector addition is commutative and associative. Scalar multiplication scales the magnitude without changing direction (unless the scalar is negative, which reverses direction). These operations form the algebraic foundation of vector spaces.

nodes.label: Dot Product
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The dot product of two vectors a·b = |a||b|cosθ = Σaᵢbᵢ. It produces a scalar. Key property: if a·b = 0, the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular). The dot product measures how much two vectors point in the same direction. It is used to find angles between vectors, compute projections, and test orthogonality.

nodes.label: Cross Product
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The cross product a×b produces a vector perpendicular to both a and b with magnitude |a||b|sinθ. Only defined in R³. The result's direction follows the right-hand rule. |a×b| equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b. If a×b = 0, the vectors are parallel. It is anti-commutative: a×b = −(b×a).

nodes.label: Linear Combinations and Span
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A linear combination of vectors is c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ... + cₙvₙ where cᵢ are scalars. The span of a set of vectors is all possible linear combinations — it is a subspace. Understanding span is critical for understanding what vectors can and cannot reach.

nodes.label: Linear Independence
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Vectors v₁,...,vₙ are linearly independent if the only solution to c₁v₁+...+cₙvₙ=0 is c₁=c₂=...=cₙ=0. Intuitively: no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. A set is linearly dependent if any vector is redundant. Independence is a prerequisite for forming a basis.

nodes.label: Matrices
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns. Matrices represent linear transformations, systems of equations, and data. Matrix addition is component-wise. Scalar multiplication scales every entry. The transpose of A (written Aᵀ) flips rows and columns.

nodes.label: Matrix Multiplication
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Matrix multiplication (AB)ᵢⱼ = row i of A · column j of B (dot product). An m×n matrix times an n×p matrix produces an m×p matrix. Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB ≠ BA in general. It IS associative: (AB)C = A(BC). It represents composition of linear transformations.

nodes.label: Determinant
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The determinant det(A) is a scalar encoding properties of a square matrix. |det(A)| gives the volume scaling factor of the transformation. det(A) = 0 iff the matrix is singular (non-invertible, collapses space). det(AB) = det(A)·det(B). For 2×2: det = ad−bc. Negative determinant means orientation is reversed.

nodes.label: Matrix Inverse
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A square matrix A has an inverse A⁻¹ if and only if det(A) ≠ 0. A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I (identity matrix). The inverse undoes the transformation. For 2×2: A⁻¹ = (1/det(A))·[[d,−b],[−c,a]]. A matrix without an inverse is called singular. (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

nodes.label: Linear Transformations
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A linear transformation T: Rⁿ → Rᵐ satisfies T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u). Every linear transformation can be represented as a matrix: T(x) = Ax. Transformations include rotation, scaling, shear, reflection, and projection. The image of a transformation is its range; the kernel is the set of vectors mapped to zero.

nodes.label: Basis and Dimension
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A basis for a vector space is a linearly independent set that spans the space. The standard basis for Rⁿ is {e₁, e₂, ..., eₙ}. Every vector in the space has a unique representation as a linear combination of basis vectors. The dimension of a space equals the number of vectors in any basis. Different bases represent the same space differently.

nodes.label: Subspaces
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A subspace of Rⁿ is a subset that is closed under addition and scalar multiplication and contains the zero vector. Examples: the null space of a matrix, the column space. Every subspace has a basis and a dimension. The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix (column space, null space, row space, left null space) are central to understanding linear systems.

nodes.label: Orthogonality
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: Two vectors are orthogonal if their dot product is zero (a·b = 0). An orthogonal set has all pairs orthogonal. An orthonormal set is orthogonal with all unit vectors. Orthonormal bases are computationally convenient: the coefficients in the expansion are just dot products. The Gram-Schmidt process converts any basis to an orthonormal one.

nodes.label: Projections
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The projection of vector b onto vector a is: proj_a(b) = (a·b/|a|²)a. Projection onto a subspace V finds the closest point in V to b. Least squares solutions minimize ||Ax−b||², found via the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb. Projection is fundamental to least squares, regression, and dimensionality reduction.

nodes.label: Rank
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows (or columns) — the dimension of the column space. Rank-nullity theorem: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n (number of columns). A full-rank matrix has rank = min(m,n). Rank determines whether a linear system has solutions and whether a matrix is invertible.

nodes.label: Eigenvalues
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: An eigenvalue λ of matrix A satisfies det(A − λI) = 0 (the characteristic equation). Eigenvalues are the scalars by which eigenvectors are stretched or shrunk under the transformation. The set of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of the matrix. Trace(A) = sum of eigenvalues. det(A) = product of eigenvalues. Complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs for real matrices.

nodes.label: Eigenvectors
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: An eigenvector v of matrix A satisfies Av = λv — it is a non-zero vector that only gets scaled (not rotated) by the transformation. Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are linearly independent. Geometrically, eigenvectors point in the directions that are preserved by the transformation. They are not unique — any scalar multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector.

nodes.label: Diagonalization
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A matrix A is diagonalizable if A = PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal (eigenvalues on diagonal) and P's columns are eigenvectors. Diagonalization simplifies powers of matrices: Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹. A matrix is diagonalizable iff it has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Symmetric matrices are always diagonalizable with orthonormal eigenvectors (spectral theorem).

nodes.label: Singular Value Decomposition
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: SVD decomposes any m×n matrix A = UΣVᵀ where U and V are orthonormal matrices and Σ is diagonal with non-negative singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ ... ≥ 0. SVD works for any matrix (not just square). Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA. Applications: PCA, compression, pseudoinverse, recommendation systems, low-rank approximation.

nodes.label: Systems of Linear Equations
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A system Ax = b has: a unique solution (if A is invertible, rank = n), no solution (inconsistent, when b is not in the column space), or infinitely many solutions (when the null space is nontrivial). Gaussian elimination reduces the augmented matrix [A|b] to row echelon form. The solution set is the particular solution plus the null space.

nodes.label: Vector Spaces
nodes.subject: mathematics
nodes.description: A vector space is a set V with operations of addition and scalar multiplication satisfying 8 axioms (closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverse, scalar identity, distributivity). Examples: Rⁿ, polynomial spaces, function spaces, matrix spaces. The concept generalises vectors beyond arrows in space to any objects obeying these rules.
